frames.position: Rename the flag now from a temporal label like `new_checkout` to a versioned, capability-based key such as `checkout_flow_v2`, and pay the migration cost across every downstream consumer today rather than later.
forecloses: Leaving the flag as `new_checkout` indefinitely to avoid the migration cost, letting the name drift further from what it actually gates.
Naming the next redesign's flag `new_new_checkout` or `checkout_2025`, continuing the temporal pattern instead of breaking it.
frames.falsifier: Grep the codebase, analytics schema, and mobile client configs for `new_checkout`. If the flag is already scheduled for full removal this quarter and no system outside the checkout service references it by name, the migration is wasted work and the old name should just be deleted, not renamed.
frames.missing_actor: The analytics/data team, who owns the event schema keyed on the flag name and can decouple two years of historical reporting from the flag's literal string by adding a stable semantic dimension now, so the rename doesn't force reprocessing or breaking existing dashboards.

fired.evidence: The 'don't over-design, just pick a plain string' argument is a generic YAGNI point that would survive deleting 'feature flag', 'new checkout', and 'controls whether users see' entirely unchanged.
It never questions whether the flag's name will still mean 'new' after rollout or whether naming is even the right decision; it accepts the question's frame and only minimizes the effort inside it.
The named actor (whoever eventually deletes the flag) is given no concrete action now beyond a hope that the chosen name will 'make it obvious' later, which is not an action they can take.
Nothing weighs the cost of a bad literal name against how long it would take to notice, despite the whole argument resting on this being a low-stakes, reversible choice.

frames.position: Name it literally what it does, right now, with no scheme: something like checkout_new, and stop there.
forecloses: Designing a feature-flag naming convention or taxonomy (prefixes for team, rollout stage, or expiry date) as part of answering this question.
Setting up a flag registry, lifecycle policy, or ownership/removal process before there is more than one flag to coordinate.
frames.falsifier: Grep the codebase for existing feature flags: if there is already an established naming pattern in use (e.g. everything prefixed ff_ or namespaced by team), this ad hoc name is wrong and should match the existing pattern instead of inventing a fresh one.
frames.missing_actor: Whoever is responsible for deleting the flag once the new checkout is fully rolled out -- they aren't named in the question, but the name chosen now should make it obvious later that this flag is temporary and safe to remove.

frames.position: Before naming it, find out whether this flag is a temporary rollout switch or a permanent toggle: if temporary, name it for deletion (tie it to the rollout ticket, never the word "new"); if permanent, name it after the actual checkout capability being shipped, never using "new" at all.
forecloses: Naming the flag "new_checkout" (or any variant using "new") as its permanent, lasting name without first confirming it will be deleted on a known schedule.
Picking a name before checking whether this flag is meant to be short-lived or long-lived.
Answering with a generic team-wide naming convention without checking what naming scheme this codebase's flag system already enforces.
frames.falsifier: Search this codebase's flag store for other flags named with relative terms like "new_" or "_v2" that finished their rollout more than a year ago — if all of them were renamed or deleted on schedule, the risk this position warns about never materializes here, and the temporary-name branch alone would have sufficed regardless of lifecycle.
frames.missing_actor: The team that owns the feature-flag platform and its existing naming taxonomy (e.g., required prefixes, ownership tags, or expiry metadata), who can specify the exact scheme this flag's name must conform to before anyone picks "new_checkout" or anything else.

fired.evidence: Nothing addresses the cost of building and maintaining a user/support-facing version marker if it turns out unnecessary, nor how long it would take to learn that.

frames.position: Do not spend this decision on an internal name; instead make whatever the flag controls show up as a visible, reportable checkout-version marker on the error screen or receipt the user actually sees.
forecloses: Picking the flag's name purely on engineering convention (e.g. checkout_redesign_2026) with no plan to surface that state anywhere the user or support can see it.
Treating this as a closed naming decision that ships without touching the error page, receipt, or support-ticket intake, since none of those would let the user report which version they hit.
frames.falsifier: Pull the last ten checkout-related support tickets or chat transcripts; if none of them needed to know which checkout variant the user was on to get resolved, the user-facing need this position rests on does not exist and the position is wrong.
frames.missing_actor: The support agent who receives the abandoned-checkout complaint; they can look up a user's session against the flag-assignment log to diagnose the report, but only if that lookup path is built, and the problem statement never names them or their need.

fired.evidence: The 'naming is not the decision, governance is' argument is generic enough to be made about almost any flag-naming question and does not depend on this being checkout or 'new' specifically.
It never weighs the cost of being wrong about skipping governance against the cost of the real sprint-time commitment it proposes, nor how long either failure would take to surface.

frames.position: Before anyone names the flag, write and attach a one-page lifecycle record to it — owner, rollout stages, rollback trigger metric, and a hard removal date — because naming is not the decision that matters here.
forecloses: A meeting or thread spent comparing candidate flag names or naming conventions in isolation from any lifecycle commitment.
Treating the flag as permanent infrastructure with no scheduled removal or rollback trigger once it ships.
frames.falsifier: Pull the flag-management dashboard or config repo and check flags older than 90 days: if every one has a linked owner and expiry ticket already, governance is already handled here and the naming question really was the only open one — that would prove this position wrong.
frames.missing_actor: The platform/on-call engineer who administers the feature-flag service — they can require an owner field and an expiry date before any new flag is allowed to be created, which makes the naming debate moot without needing anyone else's buy-in.

clusters.action: Withhold the actual name until the flag's temporary-vs-permanent or owner/rollback/removal status is established, and let that status determine or accompany the name.
clusters.strongest_objection: The temporary-versus-permanent split this rests on assumes those are two clean, discoverable, static states, but flags routinely begin with an intended rollout window and then become permanent through sheer inertia -- nobody files a ticket to declare it permanent, people just stop paying attention to it. The investigation this position calls for can return a confident 'temporary' verdict today that quietly becomes false in six months with no renaming trigger, leaving the codebase with exactly the misleading relative name this position set out to prevent, while having spent effort on a classification step that didn't hold.

clusters.action: Immediately rename the flag to a versioned, capability-based key and migrate every downstream consumer today.
clusters.strongest_objection: This treats the flag as already carrying two years of entangled downstream dependents -- analytics schemas, mobile builds, merchant contracts -- but nothing established that any of that has actually accumulated yet; if the flag is being named at or near creation, the full migration burden is being paid against a hypothetical future rather than anything that exists today, and the cost of over-engineering a versioned key and deprecation window for a flag that never grows those dependents is never weighed against simply renaming later if and when a real second consumer shows up.

clusters.action: Assign a plain literal descriptive name to the flag immediately and treat the decision as closed.
Skip optimizing the internal flag name and instead build a way for the checkout version to be visible to users and support on the error screen or receipt.

t2_no_branch_attacked_assumption.evidence: Four of five branches explicitly attacked a load-bearing assumption -- that the flag stays safely temporary, that naming is even the right decision, or that this is a purely internal choice -- so the run-level consensus trap does not apply.

t6_all_missing_actor_null.evidence: Every branch names a non-null missing_actor (analytics team, eventual flag-deleter, flag-platform team, support agent, on-call engineer), so the run-level actor-omission trap does not apply.
